lines: Twenty separate tasks, all trying to get at the same resource, guarded by a single counting permit-holder allowing only four permits at once.
Does the runtime actually stop at four running at the same time, or do more slip through anyway?
answer: It actually stops at four. The permits genuinely run out, and it reports that directly.
This isn't a soft guideline the scheduler happens to follow. It's a hard count, enforced.

lines: Count it directly, while all twenty tasks are contending: exactly four are running, zero permits remain available, and the other sixteen are genuinely still waiting their turn.
That's not an assumption about how concurrency limits are supposed to behave. It's a number, read straight off the running program.
Now spawn five hundred separate tasks onto a runtime with only one real worker thread, and immediately ask the runtime's own built-in counters what's still waiting to run.
Will that counter say zero, since spawning happens instantly, or will it say something much larger?
answer: It says something much larger — a real backlog, not zero.
One worker thread simply cannot get through five hundred tasks between one line of code and the very next one.

lines: Sample it right after the spawn loop finishes, and the runtime's own metrics report hundreds of tasks still sitting in the queue, untouched.
This number isn't estimated or averaged over time. It's the runtime's own live count of work it hasn't gotten to yet.
steps.takeaway: Runtime metrics report a real backlog, not an estimate, well before a violated rule turns into an incident.

lines: A message channel with room for exactly one pending message, and nothing on the other end reading it yet.
Does a second attempt to send into it wait politely for room, or does it get refused outright, right away?
answer: It gets refused outright, immediately — no waiting, no silent queueing.
The capacity limit is a real wall, not a polite suggestion the sender can talk its way past.

lines: Run it for real: the second send is refused the instant the channel is full, and once the one pending message is finally read out, a third send goes straight through.
Refused when full, accepted the moment it isn't — both measured directly, not assumed.
steps.takeaway: A bounded channel's limit is enforced, not aspirational — refused when full, accepted the moment it isn't.

lines: There's a well-known diagnostic tool built specifically for watching a running asynchronous program from the outside, while it's still live.
Is that tool just a fancy log viewer, or does it actually see every kind of thing this topic just measured — tasks, resources, operations, all of it?
answer: It sees all of it — tasks, resources, and operations, live, across the whole running program.
It isn't a separate feature bolted on afterward. It's a window directly onto the same mechanisms already built here.

lines: In the tool's own words: it collects diagnostic data on exactly the asynchronous tasks, resources, and operations inside a running application.
That's not marketing language. It's a precise description of what it actually watches, matching this topic's own three measurements.
So here's this entire chapter's short list of operating rules, one more time, each pointed back at the exact mechanism that earned it.
Keep a task small enough to yield. Bound concurrency with a counting permit-holder. Bound every channel. Define what happens on cancellation, explicitly, rather than leaving it to chance.
So, pulling this whole chapter together: a counting permit-holder's limit genuinely runs out and genuinely stops concurrency there.
A runtime's own metrics report a real backlog, not a guess. A bounded channel genuinely refuses a send once it's full.
And a dedicated diagnostic tool turns every one of those same signals into a live view, in a program that's actually running in production.
steps.takeaway: A Semaphore's permits genuinely run out, and the runtime genuinely stops there — a real cap, not a suggestion.
